stifle

/STY-ful/ — rhymes with trifle · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To stifle something is to hold it back before it can come out, such as a yawn, a laugh, or a feeling rising inside you.

She stifled a yawn during the long awards speech.

Example

During the tense confrontation, he stifled his anger, speaking quietly instead of shouting.

Stifle is precise because it emphasizes the act of holding back an emotion that wants to come out — not just feeling calm, but actively suppressing something that's rising inside. The word captures the internal struggle. Plain 'held in' would be weaker and less vivid.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

muffle: To muffle a sound is to soften or deaden it with something in the way - a scarf over a bell, a thick wall, a closed door. Stifle is about the source rather than the path: you stifle a laugh before it leaves your throat, but you muffle a noise already loose in the world.

restrain: To restrain is to physically hold a person or animal back - grabbing a leash, blocking a lunge, gripping an arm. Stifle turns that same fight inward: instead of holding a struggling body still, you stifle your own rising yawn, laugh, or sharp reply before it can escape.

smother: To smother something is to put it out by covering it and cutting off its air - flames under a blanket, a giggle behind a pressed palm. Stifle is the same clamp applied from within: to stifle is to choke back the yawn or protest rising in you before it ever reaches the air.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

express: to let a thought or feeling out

vent: to release pent-up feelings openly and freely

Where it sits · how completely the feeling is choked off

conceal → suppress → stifle → repress

conceal vs. stifle: Conceal is weaker than stifle: concealing a feeling just hides it from view, while stifling it actively chokes it back before it can escape at all.

suppress vs. stifle: Suppress is slightly weaker than stifle — suppressing holds a reaction down, but stifling squeezes it off entirely, like smothering a laugh with your hand.

repress vs. stifle: Repress is stronger than stifle: to stifle a feeling is to hold it back in the moment, while to repress it is to push it down so deep it may never surface at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — stifle (Middle English stuflen): to choke, to smother (Middle English, possibly from Old French estouffer ('to smother'))

Put it together: Stifle can't be broken into meaningful parts — it came into English whole, from a Middle English word for struggling to breathe, likely borrowed from Old French estouffer, 'to smother.' From choking off breath, its meaning stretched to choking off anything trying to come out: a yawn, a laugh, a protest.

Use the root in a new word: stuff: Stifle and stuff may both trace back to an old word for the padding used to plug things up — when you stifle a laugh, you plug it up before it can escape.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral / informal

Stifle is vivid and captures the specific action of holding back a sound or emotion that's trying to come out — not just being calm, but actively fighting to keep it in. Use it when the struggle or the emergence is the point. For simply not saying something, the plain words 'keep quiet' or 'hold back' are more neutral.
